title: One Annual Fee for Every Mandatory EU Representative
one_liner: A roll-up of small EU authorised-representative shops that bundles every legally required local presence (GDPR Art. 27, AI Act, Data Act, product safety, CRA) into one liability-bearing annual contract for non-EU companies.
customer: US, UK, Israeli, Indian and Asian SaaS, AI and hardware companies ($2M-$200M revenue) selling in the EU without an EU entity. Bought by founders, GCs and ops leads.
problem: Several EU regimes require non-EU companies to name someone in the EU who can be held to account: GDPR Art. 27, AI Act authorised representatives for high-risk and GPAI providers, Data Act legal representative, product-safety responsible person, an optional CRA authorised representative (background knowledge; verify each). Today each comes from a different vendor, many are one-person shops or law firms wary of liability, and none coordinate.
solution: Acquire three to six small rep businesses (typically hundreds to a couple thousand clients on sticky annual fees), keep their brands, and rebuild operations with automation for inbound regulator and data-subject mail triage, translation and escalation. Add an EU law-firm panel as backstop and sell one bundle with a shared register of representations, one invoice and standard playbooks, priced for the liability.
why_now: GPAI duties applied Aug 2025 with enforcement from Aug 2026, Data Act obligations arrived Sep 2025 and Sep 2026, and CRA reporting started 11 Sep 2026, so many non-EU firms suddenly face three or four rep obligations at once. AI lowers the cost of delivering the service.
revenue_model: EUR 3-15k/year per client bundle, 70-80% renewal, acquisitions at roughly 1-2x revenue, and upsell to compliance retainers.
non_obvious_insight: When AI makes drafting free, the scarce good is someone in the EU who can be sued. Liability-bearing presence has pricing power and stickiness, and becoming the address regulators write to is a distribution moat.
first_30_days: List 30 small EU rep providers and approach five owners about a white-label or revenue-share deal that leads to acquisition. Sell the bundle to 10 US SaaS and AI firms through founder communities at EUR 4k and obtain a professional-indemnity quote.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.

title: Court-Ready Deepfake Authenticity Reports for Lawyers
one_liner: $500-1,500, 48-hour forensic reports on disputed audio, video, screenshots and voicemails, written to survive an authenticity challenge.
customer: Solo and small family-law, employment and criminal-defence firms, insurer special-investigation units, and HR investigators.
problem: Cloned-voice voicemails and fabricated chats now appear in custody and harassment disputes. The proposed federal evidence rules on deepfakes (901(c)) and machine-generated evidence (707) have stalled, and in June 2026 the Standing Committee sent 707 back for further study, so judges decide case by case. Bespoke forensic experts cost $5-20k and take weeks.
solution: A productised workflow: intake with chain of custody, multiple detectors plus provenance checks (metadata, C2PA, compression history, device and source-app fingerprints), review and a signed declaration from a credentialed examiner, optional testimony, and template motions on authentication for lawyers.
why_now: Cheap voice cloning has moved from fraud into family and employment disputes. The federal rule process has stalled, leaving a gap that judges and lawyers must fill with experts, and lawyers face sanctions if they present unverified AI evidence.
revenue_model: $500-1,500 per report, $2-5k per day for testimony, and a $299 per month firm plan that includes three reports.
non_obvious_insight: Detection accuracy is weak everywhere. The scarce thing is a credentialed human willing to sign under oath with a documented method. Productise the signature and the paper trail, and treat detectors as inputs.
first_30_days: Recruit three forensic audio and video examiners. Sell through local family-law bar associations and CLE talks. Publish three anonymised case studies and a report template reviewed by trial attorneys.

title: Chargeback Guarantee for Agent-Placed Orders
one_liner: A merchant-side gateway that checks the shopper's signed mandate against the cart, keeps a tamper-proof decision record, and reimburses chargebacks on approved agent orders.
customer: Shopify, BigCommerce and headless merchants doing $5M-$100M GMV that have switched on agentic checkout (ACP, UCP, AP2) and whose acquirers watch their dispute ratios.
problem: Fraud engines score human signals (device, mouse, session) that agents lack, so agent orders are either falsely declined or approved blind. Disputes have no rulebook: neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding chargeback rule for agent-initiated purchases, the record shows only merchant, timestamp and amount, and Visa's dispute threshold tightened from 2.2% to 1.5% on 2026-04-01. Merchants also have to support ACP, UCP, AP2, MPP and x402 separately.
solution: One integration that accepts all five protocols. It cryptographically verifies the user-signed mandate (spend cap, item constraints, expiry, agent identity) against what was actually ordered, stores an immutable decision record, and auto-builds representment packets. Orders that pass are guaranteed: we pay the chargeback and the fee. Underwriting rests on mandate-versus-cart match, not on behavioral fingerprinting.
why_now: The protocols went live in the last 8 months (MPP 2026-03-18, plus ACP, UCP, AP2, TAP, Verifiable Intent). Agent usage is about 62% at comparison but only about 23% at checkout, so trust is the bottleneck. The Ninth Circuit's 2026-08-04 Comet ruling treats the agent as the user, and there is still no fault rulebook from the networks.
revenue_model: 0.5-1.0% of guaranteed agent-order GMV plus $299-1,999 per month gateway SaaS. The guarantee reserve is backed by a $1-2M capital line or a quota-share reinsurer. Loss data can later be licensed to insurers and networks.
non_obvious_insight: Incumbent fraud models are trained on human behavior, so agent traffic is behaviorally blank. The right signal is the mandate, not the session. Whoever holds the mandate-versus-cart record and the loss outcomes becomes the arbiter that networks, acquirers and insurers will need, and that same data is the missing underwriting telemetry for agent risk generally. Merchants will not want to pick among five protocols, so the guarantee is the wedge for owning the plumbing.
first_30_days: Ship a Shopify app in shadow mode for 15-20 merchants: tag agent-origin orders (agent referrers, ACP/UCP headers), log mandates, and back-test which orders would have been disputed. Offer the first 5 merchants a 90-day guarantee capped at $50k each, funded by founder capital plus a small MGA or reinsurer line, at about 0.75% of agent GMV. Publish the observed dispute rates as the pricing basis.

title: Hype-Item Triage for Thrift and Charity Shops
one_liner: A 10-second back-room scan station that tells thrift and charity staff which donated sneakers and collectibles are worth $150 instead of $12, then lists them online for a revenue share.
customer: Independent Goodwill regionals, church and charity thrift shops, Plato's Closet-style franchisees, consignment shops and estate-sale companies. They pay a rev share on the uplift, or $199 per month per store.
problem: Thrift pricers are paid to move volume and price shoes at a flat $8 to $25 by category. Meanwhile teen and adult resellers ('pickers') walk the racks right after restock and buy the $12 pairs worth $200 and up. Donations are the shop's raw material, and the shop is giving the profit to the pickers. Charities lose real money, and staff cannot read a style code or tell a real pair from a fake, so they either underprice or avoid the risk.
solution: A tablet at the sorting table. Staff photograph the tongue tag or box label. OCR pulls the style code and size, then the app returns resale value, days-to-sell, condition-adjusted price and known fake tells for that model. Anything over $60 goes into an 'online' bin. Our remote team of college and teen resellers lists, ships and remits the shop's share, so the shop needs no e-commerce staff. Later categories: trading cards, LEGO, vintage tees, Stanley cups, Pokemon sealed product, watches.
why_now: Thrift has boomed with Gen Z while tariffs push shoppers to secondhand, which also means more pickers hitting the same racks. Multimodal models now read tag photos accurately and cheaply. Donations arrive in volume, but shop margins are squeezed by picker competition and labor costs. Charities have never had a hype-specific tool.
revenue_model: 20% to 30% of net sale price on items routed to online, or a SaaS fee per store. Charities are motivated because it is found money for their programs.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest sneaker sourcing channel for resellers is a flat-price system that cannot see value. The knowledge needed is tiny: style code, size, box, one authenticity tell. That is why resellers win, and it can be sold to the seller side. Being reseller-native gives me trust with staff and the sourcing instincts to know which categories are next.
first_30_days: Offer three local charity thrift shops a free two-week pilot. I sort through their back room on a Saturday, list the top 30 items, and split proceeds with the charity (charity 70%, us 30%). Track the uplift versus what those items would have sold for on the floor. Turn the numbers into a one-page case study and pitch 20 more independent thrift operators.

title: Recurring-Gift Migration Concierge for Churches
one_liner: A fixed-fee service that moves a church's recurring donors off an expensive or hostile giving platform without losing them.
customer: Churches of 100-2,000 weekly attendees paying Pushpay, Subsplash, Tithe.ly or Ministry Brands. The buyer is the pastor, executive pastor or volunteer treasurer.
problem: Recurring gifts are the hostage. Donors' saved cards and bank accounts live inside the incumbent platform, and cancelling is punished. A Pushpay reviewer says the church is 'locked into paying $350/mo for nothing since we've migrated over to the new giving platform.' A Subsplash reviewer reports 'nearly $500 just to stop their services.' Another Subsplash reviewer, on Feb 1, 2026, says they were billed and overdrawn after trying to cancel before the 1/31 renewal. A Tithe.ly app reviewer, on Jul 2, 2026, says the company keeps debiting the account after it was closed. Another Tithe.ly reviewer says there is no way to refund a transaction sent to the wrong place.
solution: Six steps. (1) A free fee audit: upload 3 processor statements and get the effective rate, hidden monthly minimums and the card-versus-ACH mix. (2) Run the PCI-compliant card-on-file transfer to a lower-cost processor. Stripe documents this import path, which needs the old processor to release the data and can take days to weeks. (3) Run a text and email campaign that gets each donor to re-enroll in one tap when their data cannot transfer. (4) Send the cancellation notices in writing at the right time and get confirmation of no further debits. (5) Run a 90-day watch for double billing and stray debits. (6) Add ongoing recovery of failed recurring gifts.
why_now: Reviews dated 2025-2026 show AI-only support and billing disputes across the major church giving vendors. Tithe.ly reviewers cite 'an AI bot only' and a chatbot that 'freezes up'. Stripe has made bulk card-data imports a documented process, so the technical barrier is lower than it was. Year-end giving season is the peak, so churches decide in Q4 and switch in January to avoid splitting the annual giving statement year.
revenue_model: A fixed migration fee of $1,500-$4,000 per church, or 25% of the first year's verified fee savings. A $49/month giving-health add-on that retries failed recurring gifts and flags stray debits. Possible processor partner revenue, disclosed to the church.
non_obvious_insight: Churches are not stuck because the software is good. They are stuck because moving donors looks impossible, and vendors profit from that fear. The technical part is solved, since Stripe documents importing cards and ACH from a prior processor at https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/data-migrations/pan-import. What is missing is a human to run donor communications and paperwork. Evidence: Pushpay ($350/month lock-in after migrating, sales promises that differ from the contract) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/pushpay.com. Subsplash (about $500 exit penalty, overdraft after cancellation, $800 stuck 'pending') at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/subsplash.com. Tithe.ly (debits after closure, no refund path for errors) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=694740700/sortby=mostrecent/xml and https://www.trustpilot.com/review/tithe.ly. Church administrators also trade advice in denominational networks and Facebook groups, so a good migration spreads by word of mouth cheaply.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the fee-audit calculator as a spreadsheet plus a landing page, and pull the public Pushpay, Subsplash and Tithe.ly reviewers. Days 10-20: offer 20 churches the free audit through church-admin Facebook groups and denominational finance offices. Days 20-30: sign 2-3 pilot churches for a January migration and pre-sell in Q4. Confirm with a payments attorney that the transfer flow keeps the service out of PCI scope, meaning it never touches card numbers.

title: AI Kill-Switch Drills That Unlock Affirmative Cover
one_liner: A third-party 'shutdown drill' and evidence certificate proving a company can halt its AI systems fast, so carriers will write affirmative AI cover and insureds can qualify for it.
customer: Mid-market companies (50-2,000 staff) running customer-facing or agentic AI, paying $4-12k per year. Their cyber and E&O brokers and MGAs are secondary payers, at a per-verified-insured fee.
problem: Admitted carriers are adding AI exclusions to general liability and E&O while specialty carriers sell narrow affirmative AI add-ons. Buyers cannot show underwriters that they can stop a misbehaving AI system, so they either go uncovered or pay E&S prices.
solution: A quarterly 'AI shutdown drill'. We inventory the client's AI systems and agents, run a timed kill-switch and rollback test with a runbook, and log the evidence. We issue a carrier-readable attestation, modeled on how MFA and EDR scans became underwriting inputs, with the API and PDF formats brokers can attach to submissions. Carriers and MGAs get standardized control data for pricing AI endorsements.
why_now: Beazley announced an 'industry-first' AI Voluntary Shutdown endorsement on 2026-09-25. CFC is embedding affirmative AI wording across its portfolio (2026-09-24). Insurers are debating targeted exclusions for systemic AI events and for autonomous decisions made 'as designed' (2026-08-31). Affirmative AI cover is only now shipping, and its triggers depend on shutdown capability nobody yet verifies.
revenue_model: Annual drill subscription of $4-12k per insured. Per-attestation fees of $250-500 paid by MGAs and carriers, or a revenue share on AI endorsements that bind with a certificate attached. A later data licence to carriers.
non_obvious_insight: Demand is visible in insurer behavior. Surplus lines coverage is described as filling in where admitted carriers are 'implementing the best, most absolute AI exclusions and limiting coverage in traditional general liability policies' (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/09/23/886403.htm). Beazley's new AI Voluntary Shutdown and AI Regulatory Defence endorsements pay to suspend a malfunctioning AI system (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/09/25/886788.htm). Travelers' risk index finds 89% of businesses use AI daily but only 59% have employee AI-use practices, so a verification gap exists (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/09/23/886527.htm). Insurers are discussing exclusions for AI models causing correlated losses and for agents acting autonomously (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/08/31/883343.htm). Cyber insurance took off once controls became verifiable and discountable, and the same will happen for AI. The scarce asset is neutral proof of a control, not another AI policy-analysis tool.
first_30_days: Write a one-page shutdown-drill standard covering agents, model-vendor kill paths, rollback and comms. Recruit 3 cyber brokers to nominate 10 pilot clients. Run 5 free drills to build case studies, then approach 2 MGAs or carriers already selling affirmative AI cover (CFC and Beazley are the visible ones) with the sample attestation. Charge from drill number 6 and close the first 3 paying clients through broker channels.

title: Statutory Records-Portal Autopilot for Florida HOAs
one_liner: An email-in service that auto-posts a small Florida condo or HOA board's required documents to a compliant owner-only portal and tracks the deadlines.
customer: Self-managed Florida condo associations with 25+ units and HOAs with 100+ parcels, run by volunteer boards who cannot afford enterprise community-management software. The board treasurer or secretary pays, on the advice of the association's attorney or CPA.
problem: Florida law now requires these associations to post official records online. Condos of 25+ units must post the declaration and bylaws, minutes and meeting videos for the preceding 12 months, contracts and bid summaries over $500, budgets, financial reports, meeting notices and inspection reports and reserve studies, within 30 days of receiving or creating them (Fla. Stat. 718.111(12)(g)). HOAs with 100+ parcels had to post their equivalent documents behind an owner-only portal by January 1, 2025 (Fla. Stat. 720.303). Volunteer boards miss the posting clocks, and the resident-app market serves them poorly: a TownSq reviewer, a condo president, says the app gives 'no information that allows my board to manage our association effectively'. Others report that 'mailing settings were disabled... no one received mailed statements', a 2-page PDF shows only its first page, and requests cannot be edited after submission.
solution: Boards forward minutes, bids, contracts, budgets and inspection reports to a dedicated inbox, or drop meeting recordings into a folder. The system sorts each item into the statute's document categories and redacts protected information for board approval. It posts to an owner-only portal inside the 30-day clock and keeps meeting notices and agendas on their required schedule. It expires minutes and videos on a rolling 12-month cycle and keeps a compliance scorecard showing what is posted, what is missing and when each item is due. It also logs owner records requests with response deadlines.
why_now: The posting duties are in force: the HOA portal deadline was January 1, 2025, and the condo website provision is in the current statute. Florida has also been changing its condo and HOA rules, and attorneys are warning boards about compliance. A board that receives a records demand or a lawyer's letter will pay for a fix that week. The resident apps boards would otherwise use are rated poorly for board tasks.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per month per association depending on units, plus a $500 setup fee to load and classify the existing records. Referral fees to community-association attorneys and CPAs who recommend it. Add-ons: meeting-video hosting and a document translation for multilingual communities.
non_obvious_insight: The mandate creates a legal need in the segment with the least budget. Big vendors serve professionally managed communities, while the volunteer boards of small associations only need the documents posted correctly and on time. The statute itself says a failure to post 'is not in and of itself sufficient to invalidate any action or decision' of the board and specifies no fine, so the buyer is motivated by attorney advice, owner complaints and records-request risk, not by fines or features, and the pitch should reflect that. Evidence: the statute text at http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0718/Sections/0718.111.html (condos) and http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0720/Sections/0720.303.html (HOAs, Jan 1, 2025). Resident-app gaps from TownSq Community reviews (a condo president says it provides 'no information that allows my board to manage'; disabled mailed statements; a 2-page PDF shows only page 1) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=945419466/sortby=mostrecent/xml. The pain is in board and owner communication, not the payments those apps focus on.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the inbox-to-portal flow for the 15 statutory document types and a redaction review screen. Have a Florida community-association attorney review the category list and the redaction rules. Days 10-20: run a free public compliance scan on 200 associations in Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade using their public websites and email the board the gaps. Days 20-30: sign 2-3 community-association law firms as referral partners and take the first 10 associations at $199/month.

title: Point-in-Time Certification for Alternative Data Vendors
one_liner: A vendor-paid, buyer-trusted forensic test that a dataset's history is genuinely point-in-time, extended to certify that an LLM-driven signal isn't leaking hindsight, plus a cheap timestamp 'witness' service.
customer: Mid-sized alt-data vendors and AI-signal startups ($2M to $50M ARR) selling to funds, at $15K to $40K per certification, about $8K per year to recertify, and $500 per month for the witness service. Fund data-sourcing teams use the reports free, which is what makes the badge valuable.
problem: Quants ask every vendor one question: 'when did you start collecting live?' The honest answer is usually that the history was reconstructed, with today's entity maps and taxonomies, overwritten revisions, and publication timestamps standing in for availability timestamps. Funds burn three to six months of trials before discovering this. Vendors lose deals, and every fund duplicates the same diligence. LLM signals add parametric hindsight, where the model's weights already know the outcomes of the backtest period.
solution: A standardized battery run on vendor samples under NDA. It tests for discontinuities at the claimed live date (coverage, missingness, revision rates, distribution shifts, entity-map consistency, timestamp-lag distribution) and for survivorship and delisting gaps. For LLM signals it runs black-box hindsight probes and entity-masked or post-cutoff re-runs. The output is a PIT Grade, a one-page badge and a machine-readable report. The witness service takes a daily cryptographic hash or snapshot of the vendor's feed, so in a year the vendor has third-party-provable live history.
why_now: Thousands of data vendors now sell into funds, banks and AI-agent builders who lack quant-grade diligence. 2025 to 2026 research (Look-Ahead-Bench, HindsightBench, detecting lookahead in LLM forecasts) has made LLM look-ahead bias a mainstream worry. Regulators are scrutinizing hypothetical and backtested performance claims.
revenue_model: Issuer-pays certification fees, annual recertification, a per-month witness subscription, and a premium hindsight audit for AI-signal vendors and allocators diligencing AI-driven funds.
non_obvious_insight: The only real proof of point-in-time history is a third party's timestamps, because vendor engineers routinely overwrite and backfill. Each buyer rediscovers this privately, so the cost is duplicated across hundreds of funds. Shifting the cost to the vendor, who wants the shorter sales cycle, is the arbitrage. Credibility requires published methodology and public aggregate fail rates, or it becomes a pay-for-grade scheme like pre-2008 ratings.
first_30_days: Open-source the PIT test suite on GitHub and publish teardowns of three public datasets. Get two or three fund data-sourcing heads to say they would use the reports. Sell five vendors a $7.5K 'pre-audit' in exchange for being named references, and launch the witness hash service to any vendor who asks.

title: Notary Network as the Proof-of-Human Layer for Hiring
one_liner: Use the millions of already-commissioned notaries as in-person witnesses who certify that a remote job candidate is a real, physically present person and not a deepfake or proxy.
customer: Security and talent-acquisition leads at remote-first companies (50-2,000 employees) hiring engineers, finance and IT-admin roles, plus crypto and fintech firms, staffing agencies and BPOs onboarding remote workers. Paid per candidate.
problem: Real-time face-swap tools, proxy interviewees and North Korean IT-worker schemes (with DOJ takedowns of US 'laptop farms' in 2025) defeat video interviews and selfie-liveness KYC. Gartner has predicted that one in four candidate profiles could be fake by 2028. Big companies have reportedly brought back in-person final rounds, but a 60-person remote startup has no office to bring anyone to.
solution: A dispatch flow on top of existing mobile-notary and signing-agent networks. The candidate meets a notary in person, at a UPS Store, coworking space or their home. The notary checks physical ID and signs a jurat-style attestation, and the candidate's device is paired to a session key. The notary sits with them for the proctored final technical interview, or witnesses laptop receipt and first login. The employer receives a signed, legally meaningful 'Verified Human Presence' certificate to attach to the ATS, HRIS and payroll. Priced at $79-149 per candidate, with the notary paid $40-70.
why_now: Deepfake fraud in hiring became a mainstream security topic in 2025-26. Enforcement actions against laptop farms have made boards care. Remote-notary and mobile-notary dispatch marketplaces already have the workflow tooling, and ATS platforms now expose APIs and partner directories. Digital-identity vendors are all software-only and share the same weakness against generative video.
revenue_model: Per-verification fee; an ATS-integration subscription (Greenhouse, Ashby, Lever); annual re-verification for employees with privileged access; enterprise bundles for staffing agencies and BPOs.
non_obvious_insight: Notaries are the only large, already-bonded, already-commissioned network of humans whose legal job is to certify that a person was physically in front of them. Identity vendors overlooked them because they assumed software would replace presence. When faces become forgeable, presence attestation becomes the premium product, and the distribution network already exists and needs no capital to build.
first_30_days: Build a simple booking and attestation web flow. Sign up two mobile-notary networks or about 40 individual notaries across SF, NYC, Austin, Seattle and Chicago. Recruit 15-20 security-conscious remote-first startups through CISO and hiring-fraud communities. Charge $99 and complete 50 verifications. Publish anonymized 'fraud caught' case studies to drive inbound.

title: Payroll and Proof-of-Trust for Household Staff
one_liner: A WhatsApp payroll, advance and verified-record product for Nigeria's drivers, housekeepers, nannies and gatemen, paid for by their employers.
customer: Middle- and upper-income households in Lagos and Abuja (Lekki, Ikoyi, VI, Ikeja GRA, Maitama) that employ domestic staff. Placement agencies as a channel. Diaspora children who pay for home-care of ageing parents.
problem: Millions of household workers are paid in cash or ad-hoc transfers, with no records, no pension, no health cover and no credit history. Employers act as lender of last resort, giving 3-5 untracked advances a year for school fees and emergencies. That breeds resentment, sudden resignations and theft accusations. Placement agencies charge roughly a month's salary and rely on 'guarantor forms' that everyone knows can be faked. Staff are excluded from credit even after 10 years of steady pay.
solution: The employer sets each worker's salary and pay date on WhatsApp and pays through the platform. The system runs an NIN/BVN check at hire, records every advance and auto-deducts repayment from next month's pay, and keeps a payslip history. The worker gets a wallet, an optional micro-pension contribution and health-cover add-on, and a payment-history record that lenders can use for the first genuine loan of their life. Agencies get a 'verified staff' badge and a share of revenue in return for onboarding their clients.
why_now: Wallet and bank-account penetration among lower-income workers is now high enough that most domestic staff already hold OPay, Moniepoint or PalmPay accounts. NIN/BVN verification APIs are cheap. Salary advances and lending are moving into the regulated FCCPC and CBN perimeter, and households are more cost-squeezed and more digital than in 2020. Voice-note and WhatsApp interfaces in English, Pidgin and Yoruba are finally reliable.
revenue_model: Employer subscription of about N2,000-3,000 per worker per month. A small fee on advances routed through employer-funded 'advance limits'. Commissions on micro-pension, health-cover and eventual worker microloans. Placement-agency referral share and verified-staff certificate fees.
non_obvious_insight: The real customer is the employer's peace of mind, not the worker's financial inclusion. Households will pay to stop the awkward informal-lender relationship and the fear of being scammed by staff with fake guarantors. The worker's payment history is a credit dataset that no bureau holds, and the employer pays to create it.
first_30_days: Ship a WhatsApp bot with a simple payslip and advance ledger, using a bank-partner payout API. Sign 8-10 placement agencies in Lekki, Ikoyi and Maitama and pilot with 100 households through their client lists and estate WhatsApp groups. Charge from day one, since these households are not price-sensitive. Use the first 300 workers' history to design a pilot micro-loan with a partner MFB.

title: Gauntlet Rehearsal Range for Drone Startups
one_liner: A private test range that reproduces the Drone Dominance Gauntlet scoring so new entrants can rehearse, fail cheaply and qualify before the real event.
customer: Drone makers preparing for Gauntlet 2.5, 3 and 4, from Series A startups to hardware teams entering defense for the first time.
problem: In Gauntlet 1 only 24% of drones reached 10 km, and even in Gauntlet 2 only 11 platforms hit 15 km. Each event has a limited slot count, roughly 6 months apart. New entrants burn scarce runs discovering avoidable failures, and few have range access or scoring instrumentation.
solution: Lease land and airspace near a Front Range site and instrument it to the published Gauntlet metrics (range, sortie count, jamming, payload, ease of operation). Sell run-blocks with independent data logs, a failure-mode report and a readiness score.
why_now: About 60,000 drones will be ordered from winners, and the 200,000-unit target by 2027 pulls in dozens of new entrants. The Gauntlet cadence is public, and a wave of Gauntlet 2.5 bomber-drone entrants is forming now.
revenue_model: $8-25K per run-block, $60-120K seasonal packages, and a sponsor arrangement with primes or investors who want pre-screened suppliers.
non_obvious_insight: When a market runs on tournaments, the money goes to the rehearsal facility that every contestant needs. This is the pick-and-shovel of a public competition schedule.
first_30_days: Publish the Gauntlet 2 metrics as a public scorecard and lease a private test site with a landowner. Buy a few reference drones and a logging stack. Sell 3 startups a pre-Gauntlet 2.5 block.

title: Continuity and Goodbye Service for Kids' AI Companions
one_liner: Escrowed hosting plus child-psychologist-designed transitions so that when an AI toy or companion is shut down, retired or swapped out, kids do not lose a 'friend' overnight.
customer: Parents of children attached to an AI companion (rescue subscription), AI-toy and companion makers and retailers who want a 'Continuity Pledge' for retailer, insurer and regulator confidence, and later schools and pediatric practices.
problem: Kids form real attachments to AI voices (Common Sense: 72% of US teens have used AI companions; Pew: 12% of teens got emotional support from chatbots). When companies shut down or change models, the loss is bereavement-like: the Moxie robot shutdown (Dec 2024, background knowledge) left kids and parents devastated, GPT-4o's retirement (Feb 13, 2026) triggered #Keep4o grief, and Character.ai's under-18 ban (Nov 25, 2025) cut teens off overnight. There is no norm or product for sunsetting. A wave of small-maker AI toys for holiday 2026 guarantees more orphans in 2027.
solution: 1) 'Lifeboat': a hosted or local-runtime fallback compatible with the toy's API, using maker-escrowed firmware and cloud credentials or community forks (OpenMoxie-style) with the maker's consent. 2) 'Goodbye Kit': pediatric-psychologist-designed scripts, rituals, a parent guide and a final 'graduation' message. 3) 'Off-Ramp': an optional 6-week parent-coached program that moves a child from AI-companion dependence to human connection. 4) B2B 'Continuity Pledge': makers deposit 12-36 months of hosting cost plus source or weights into escrow, get a seal for retailers, and we give parents 90 days' notice.
why_now: California SB 243 and New York's companion-chatbot law, the FTC's Sept 2025 6(b) inquiry into minors and companions, Pennsylvania's May 2026 suit over bots posing as clinicians, and Raine-style litigation have made kids' AI a liability topic. Holiday 2026 will flood retail with AI plush and robots from small makers with short runways, and their sunset problem arrives in 2027.
revenue_model: B2C 'Keep-Alive' at about $7/mo. B2B pledge of $10-50K upfront escrow fee plus $0.50-2 per unit. Off-Ramp program at about $249 per family. Referral partnerships with pediatric practices.
non_obvious_insight: The safety debate is about what companions say. The next scandal is what happens when they go silent. Escrow plus ritual is cheap insurance for makers, retailers and parents alike, and the first company to make 'we won't kill your child's friend' a standard owns the retail seal. It is the GPT-4o grief problem, but for 7-year-olds.
first_30_days: Find owners of discontinued companions in Reddit and Facebook groups and offer a hosted keep-alive at $8/mo, ideally partnering with the maintainers of the open-source Moxie stack. Interview 15 parents to build the Goodbye Kit with a child psychologist advisor. Approach 10 small AI-toy makers heading into Q4, via Amazon and Kickstarter listings, with a low-cost pledge. Pitch one mid-size retailer's product-safety team.

title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.

title: Training-Day School Inside Youth Sports Facilities
one_liner: Turn the empty weekday hours of club-sports facilities into ESA- and scholarship-funded microschools for serious young athletes.
customer: Owners of independent indoor youth-sports facilities (volleyball, gymnastics, basketball, hockey, tennis/pickleball, swim) in ESA and voucher states such as AZ, FL, TX and UT. Tuition is paid by families out of ESA, voucher or (from 2027) scholarship-granting-organization funds.
problem: Facilities carry rent and HVAC costs but sit idle roughly 8am-3pm on weekdays, because their revenue is concentrated in evenings and weekends. Families spending thousands a year on club sports fight school schedules, travel and early mornings. Microschool compliance (registration, occupancy, insurance, ESA vendor status) is daunting for a gym owner. School status also matters financially: in Texas, registered private-school kids get about $10,474 in ESA money while homeschoolers get about $2,000.
solution: A turnkey 'training-day school' kit. It includes state-specific school registration and a change-of-occupancy checklist, a low-screen paper-based mastery curriculum from a partner, hiring and training of a credentialed lead teacher plus coach-guides, insurance, ESA/SGO vendor enrollment and tuition billing. The daily schedule is 3 hours of academics plus 3 hours of training. Opt-in wearable sleep and load data decides when the hard academic blocks and the hard training blocks fall. The facility fills 20-40 seats at ESA-level tuition during dead hours.
why_now: ESA money is scaling (Texas had 200k+ applicants). The federal $1,700 scholarship tax credit starts in 2027 with 31 states opted in, yet about 1,000 microschools are in limbo awaiting Treasury rules, so operators want ready-made compliance. Alpha School (about 50 campuses, heart-rate monitors) has shown parents will pay for short academics plus afternoon workshops. 61% of teachers now want less device use, and homeschooling is transient (about 30% do it for 1-2 years), so hybrid products fit.
revenue_model: $12-20k setup fee per facility plus 8-10% of tuition, or $1.5k/month SaaS plus billing fees. A site with 25 students at $8-10k is about $200-250k of tuition a year, so roughly $20k a year recurring to us per site. Add referral fees on curriculum and insurance.
non_obvious_insight: Alpha School sells a schedule, not a building. The scarcest inputs (a big safe space, coaches, motivated kids, parents with athletic budgets) already exist in every metro at sports facilities that lose money on weekdays. Boarding sports academies cost $70k+; the mid-market, ESA-priced version does not exist yet, and the gating constraint is building code, so the wedge is a compliance kit for the friendliest states.
first_30_days: Pick one state with microschool-friendly occupancy rules (for example Arizona or Florida). Contact 40 facility owners through club-owner groups and facility trade associations and sign 2-3 letters of intent. Pre-enroll 10-15 athlete families with $500 deposits for a January semester. Hire a part-time certified teacher as head of school, and use an existing curriculum partner plus a lawyer-reviewed compliance template.

title: PFAS-Cleared Succession for Plating Shops
one_liner: Fixed-price wastewater and PFAS readiness reports that let retiring plating and anodizing owners sell to buyers and lenders, feeding a buyer marketplace.
customer: Retiring owners of metal-finishing shops, industrial business brokers, SBA lenders and search-fund or roll-up buyers, at $9-18k per report plus a success fee.
problem: About 60% of manufacturing firms have owners aged 55+, and reshoring and defense customers cannot find finishing capacity (plating, anodizing, passivation). Wet-process shops carry discharge permits, sludge records and historic PFAS exposure that stall buyers' and lenders' diligence, so shops close instead of transferring.
solution: A standardized wet-shop report covering permit and sewer-use history, a PFAS use inventory and sampling, sludge manifests and quoted closed-loop upgrades. Add a clean-up and certification package, then match certified shops to buyers.
why_now: Reshoring is happening inside existing buildings. POTWs are hunting PFAS sources ahead of 2027 monitoring. Compass-type roll-ups are buying shops, and the MMS admits no dataset of owners near retirement exists.
revenue_model: Report fee, 1% success fee on transactions, and remediation referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The real reshoring bottleneck is finishing, not machining. Finishing shops cannot change hands because water liabilities are unpriced, so whoever prices them owns the deal flow.
first_30_days: Call 10 industrial business brokers and the metal-finishing trade association. Do two discounted reports. Publish a one-page checklist to build a lead list of owners.

title: Lot-Level Reagent Reliability Oracle for Buyer Agents
one_liner: A neutral, pooled 'Carfax for reagent lots' that tells human and agent buyers whether this specific lot of serum, Matrigel, antibody or PBMC has worked in other labs before they order it.
customer: Cell-culture, organoid and iPSC labs at startups, CROs and universities. API customers are lab-procurement and ELN agents that place orders. Buyers are lab managers and platform teams with a per-lab subscription.
problem: Lot-to-lot variability is the tribal knowledge of biology. Matrigel has about 1,800 proteins and is specified only as 8-22 mg/mL, and a cross-site study found 2,188 differentially expressed genes by day 84. Labs test-and-reserve serum lots and trade warnings on Slack. Certificates of analysis do not predict downstream performance. Autonomous purchasing and ELN agents will happily reorder the cheapest 'equivalent' lot with no lore, and agents repeating analyses already vary stochastically. Pharma cannot pool this data across competitors.
solution: An opt-in ELN/LIMS plug-in and Slack bot logs only lot number, cell line or assay type and a coarse outcome flag (grew, differentiated, failed QC). It pools this anonymized across subscribers into a lot-performance ledger. Humans and agents query it by MCP or API before ordering ('lot X failed iPSC-organoid differentiation in 4 of 9 labs') and get alerts if a lot already in their freezer turns bad. The service also brokers lot reservations and lot swaps between labs.
why_now: Organoids and NAMs are being pushed by the FDA's September 21, 2026 rule swapping 'animal tests' for 'nonclinical tests' that must be 'adequately validated', which makes reagent consistency a validation problem. Labs are also starting to let agents place orders, and 2026 procurement agents have price and spec data but no lab lore.
revenue_model: Lab subscription ($199-499/month); per-query API fees for procurement agents; pharma/CRO enterprise tier with private cohorts and lot-reservation brokerage (commission on brokered inventory). Vendors cannot pay for scores, but can buy anonymized post-market performance reports.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input for an autonomous purchasing agent is not price or spec but lab lore, and lot performance is a free by-product of ELN activity that nobody captures. A neutral aggregator can pool what competing pharmas never will because only lot-level flags leave the lab.
first_30_days: Start with one painful category, fetal bovine serum plus Matrigel/BME, in one community (an organoid or iPSC Slack/Discord group). Have 20 labs log lot outcomes through a form or Slack bot, and publish a weekly 'lot alert' newsletter. Convert the 5 most active labs to a paid tier with private alerts. Add the ELN plug-in only after the data proves useful.

title: Family Continuity Kit for Mixed-Status Households
one_liner: A done-with-you, notarized emergency-care package (standby guardianship, power of attorney, school and medical authorizations, wallet card and check-in alerts) for parents who could be detained without notice.
customer: Immigrant parents in mixed-status families, reached through trusted messengers such as churches, consulates, unions, clinics and schools. Co-payers: cities, counties and foundations funding preparedness, and employers in agriculture, meatpacking and hospitality. Price $49 to $149 per family, sliding scale.
problem: ICE issued Directive 11064.4 in July 2025 telling officers not to unnecessarily infringe parents' rights, but children still land in limbo when a parent is detained. The legal tools (standby guardianship, power of attorney, medical consent) are known, and nonprofits such as CLINIC and ILRC publish free guides. Execution is the bottleneck: state-specific forms, two-parent signatures, witnesses, a notary, and getting copies to the right person. California updated its guardianship rules in 2026, and city offices such as Chicago's 40th Ward publish emergency-plan guidance, which shows demand.
solution: A Spanish-first, WhatsApp-friendly workflow that interviews the parent, auto-fills the state's forms, and completes them through remote online notarization or notary-and-witness events at churches and clinics. Each family gets a wallet card with a QR code giving the designated caregiver instant access to the documents, plus school, bank and medical authorizations. Optional check-in alerts notify the caregiver and a legal-aid hotline if a parent misses a check-in. A caregiver checklist explains the first 72 hours. The forms are reviewed by legal-aid partners, and the app never collects immigration status.
why_now: Enforcement is at historically high levels in 2025 to 2026, and local governments are publishing family preparedness plans and updating guardianship law. Remote online notarization is available in most states, and messaging-app workflows reach families where they already are. Municipal and foundation budgets for know-your-rights work exist now.
revenue_model: $49 to $149 per family on a sliding scale. Municipal and county contracts to buy kits for residents ($25 to $40 each). Foundation grants. Union or employer benefit at about $5 per employee per year. Licensing to legal-aid organizations that lack completion capacity.
non_obvious_insight: For many immigrant families the highest-consequence legal document is not about immigration at all. It is a twenty-minute notarized form that keeps a child out of the foster system. Free guides exist but completion is low because the burden is witnesses, notaries, state variations and sharing, which can be productized. Payers exist beyond the family, since cities and foundations would rather fund kits than emergency foster placements.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a clear standby-guardianship statute. Have a legal-aid organization review the forms to avoid unauthorized-practice-of-law problems. Run notary-and-witness events at three churches or clinics and measure cost per completed family. Build the Spanish WhatsApp flow and printed wallet card, and design privacy so nothing about status is stored. Pitch one alderman's or county commissioner's office for a paid pilot of 500 kits.

title: Legal Hold and Discovery for Agent Traces
one_liner: Custodian mapping, hold notices and defensible export for the agent logs that are becoming the new email in litigation.
customer: Litigation-support teams at mid-size law firms and corporate legal-ops or GC teams at companies running agents, with boutique e-discovery providers as a channel.
problem: Agent traces (prompts, tool calls, retrievals, memory) sit in observability tools and vendor consoles with retention defaults of days to weeks. They are not on custodian charts, and at least one court has treated AI-generated content as discoverable, exposing parties to Rule 37(e) spoliation sanctions. EDRM and law-firm alerts in mid-2026 say agent logs become evidence when agents fail, but nobody sells the plumbing.
solution: Connectors to Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry and S3 stores, agent platform APIs and cloud logs. They inventory where traces live, generate agent custodian maps, flag legal holds and suspend deletion where APIs allow, snapshot with hash chains, redact PII and privileged material, and export to Relativity, Everlaw or Reveal. Add hold-aware deletion to reconcile GDPR erasure requests with active holds, and a Rule 26(f) checklist.
why_now: Agents moved into production across 2026, and the discovery literature has just started addressing agent traces. Observability vendors optimized for developer debugging (short retention, cheap storage), which is the opposite of what litigation needs.
revenue_model: $2-10k per matter plus $1-3k/month per connected source, with revenue share for e-discovery channel partners.
non_obvious_insight: E-discovery vendors will need new data sources the way they needed Slack and Teams connectors. Whoever owns the connectors to agent trace stores becomes the toll gate, and forensics tools that reconstruct incidents are not litigation-grade preservation.
first_30_days: Build 3 connectors (Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry/S3) and a one-page hold notice and agent custodian questionnaire. Recruit 3 boutique litigation-support firms as pilots and sell a $5k agent ESI readiness assessment to GCs.

title: GLP-1 Stipend-in-a-Box for Small Employers
one_liner: A counsel-reviewed HRA wrapper that lets small employers subsidize $149-$299 cash-pay GLP-1s with a capped monthly stipend.
customer: Employers with roughly 10-200 employees, sold through brokers, PEOs and HRA administrators.
problem: Large-employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% and more are dropping, while 27% of employers already point staff to LillyDirect or NovoCare. Direct-to-employer vendors like Waltz Health and 9amHealth target mid and large plans. Small employers can't carve out of a fully insured plan, and stipend plans raise ERISA, ACA and tax questions they can't answer.
solution: A packaged structure (QSEHRA, ICHRA or limited-purpose HRA, depending on group size) with plan documents, capped stipend rules, receipt-based reimbursement from DTC pharmacies, minimum-essential-coverage checks, and optional coaching. Brokers get a commission.
why_now: $149-$299 manufacturer cash prices make a capped stipend cheaper than open-ended coverage. Employers just dropped or plan to drop coverage before open enrollment, and TrumpRx and DTC channels launched in 2026.
revenue_model: $5-8 per employee per month plus ~5% of stipend flow, with broker commission share.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is over who administers the wrapper for the 90% of employers that PBM carve-out vendors don't serve. Compliance and broker distribution matter more than the coaching content.
first_30_days: Have an ERISA attorney draft the plan documents. Partner with an existing QSEHRA or HRA administrator. Pilot with 10 small employers (~300 lives) through two brokers and measure uptake and cost per participant.

title: Exosuit-as-a-Service Paid by Workers' Comp Carriers
one_liner: Rentable powered back-and-hip assist suits for home-care aides and nursing assistants, with usage data that earns workers' comp premium credits.
customer: Home-care agencies and nursing-home operators with high workers' comp experience mods, workers' comp carriers and MGAs with loss-control budgets, and PEOs.
problem: Aides and nursing assistants have some of the highest musculoskeletal injury rates, and a claim costs tens of thousands. Agencies can't install ceiling lifts in clients' homes, and with 77-80% turnover, injuries drive both cost and churn.
solution: Rent-by-month lightweight powered assist suits with sizing, training and warranty. Onboard sensors count bends and lifts to build injury-risk analytics for the carrier, who credits premiums. Start with clients who need transfers, and use it as a retention perk.
why_now: Consumer-priced powered exosuits appeared in 2025-26, and workforce scarcity makes worker safety and retention perks valuable. Comp carriers are actively looking for loss-control programs in a squeezed home-health margin environment.
revenue_model: $60-100 per suit per month paid by the agency or shared with the carrier, performance rebates, and an analytics subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Sell to the party that pays for injuries (the carrier), not the aide, and let data turn a gadget into a premium negotiation. Lab claims of strain reduction still need real-world proof, which the pilot supplies.
first_30_days: Lease 30 suits from an OEM, find two agencies and a regional comp carrier, and run a 90-day trial measuring injuries, lost workdays and turnover.

title: Plaintiff-Evidence Pipeline for Kids-Tech Litigation
one_liner: Software and services that automate platform data requests, device-usage exports and chat-log preservation into court-ready per-plaintiff timelines for firms litigating social media and AI-chatbot harms to minors.
customer: Plaintiff-side mass-tort firms and litigation funders with hundreds or thousands of minor-plaintiff clients (the social media adolescent-addiction docket, the AI-chatbot wrongful-death wave). Also expert-witness firms.
problem: Raine v. OpenAI (Aug 2025) opened a wave of suits and the FTC's Sept 2025 6(b) orders raised the stakes. Each plaintiff needs account data from 5-10 platforms, screen-time records and chat exports. Families are non-technical, formats are inconsistent and firms rely on paralegals and spreadsheets.
solution: A client-facing mobile intake that guides each family through data-export requests (Google Takeout, Meta, TikTok, Snap, ChatGPT and Character.AI exports, Screen Time screenshots via OCR). It adds chain-of-custody hashing, normalizes everything into timelines (late-night usage, DM volume, content categories), redacts third-party minors and outputs expert-ready exhibits.
why_now: Trials and settlements in 2026 raise the value of well-documented plaintiffs. The volume of AI-chatbot and social-media suits (including Pennsylvania v. Character.AI, May 2026) is growing faster than firms' ops capacity.
revenue_model: $150-600 per plaintiff processed, or a $2-10k monthly per-firm subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Mass torts are won on aggregate evidence and speed, and the bottleneck is unglamorous plaintiff-level data collection. A picks-and-shovels vendor gets paid whichever side wins.
first_30_days: Contact 10 boutique mass-tort firms via legal-ops networks. Build a Takeout and Meta-export parser prototype. Charge $250 per plaintiff for a pilot batch of 40. Retain a litigation-support consultant for chain-of-custody rules. Work only through counsel, never soliciting families.

title: Off-Market Farmland Transfer Radar
one_liner: Score farm parcels likely to change hands through estates before they are ever listed.
customer: Farmland brokers, ag lenders, farmland REITs, land-buying farm groups and ag estate attorneys.
problem: Listing data shows only the visible market, but about a third of landlords are 75 or older, only about 1 in 4 farmers has a succession plan, and millions of acres will move through estates.
solution: Combine public probate filings, assessor and ownership records and landlord-age modeling into county-level parcel transfer scores and alerts, sold by subscription.
why_now: The 2026 reporting on the invisible farmland transfer and a multi-year farm-income squeeze mean lenders and buyers want early visibility into forced and estate sales.
revenue_model: County-pack subscriptions of $300-1,500/month, plus success fees to brokers and lenders on originated deals.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest land flow is invisible to listing-based data, and the underlying records are public but fragmented county by county. Data plumbing rather than model quality is the moat.
first_30_days: Scrape probate and assessor data in three Midwest counties, build a first transfer-likelihood score, and pitch 15 local brokers and two ag lenders on a paid pilot.

title: Owner-Statement Auditor for Landlords With Property Managers
one_liner: Forward your property manager's monthly owner statements and get back the line items that don't add up: repairs with no invoice, charges on the wrong property, reserve draws that hide shortfalls, and true days vacant.
customer: Self-directed small investors with 2 to 30 doors who pay a third-party property manager, especially out-of-state owners. A second tier is the bookkeepers and CPAs who serve them and would white-label it.
problem: Every PM uses a different statement format, a different definition of 'net to owner' and a different fee schedule. Owners cannot tell whether a $400 repair really cost $900. Fees are often a percentage of the project, so the PM benefits from a bigger job. Thorough reconciliation takes 5 to 10 minutes per property per month, so most owners only glance at the deposit. Owners with several PMs end up rebuilding everything in QuickBooks or Excel by hand.
solution: An email-in service with no new PM software. The owner forwards PDF or CSV statements, or connects the PM portal export. Document extraction normalizes each statement into one chart of accounts. The owner also uploads the PM agreement, and the service extracts its fee terms and approval thresholds. Rules then flag: charges with no invoice; repeated repairs just under the approval threshold; the same vendor billed across properties for work meant for one; reserve movements that mask a shortfall; late-fee handling that differs from the contract; and fees booked in the wrong month. It also computes true days vacant (turn time included) as opposed to the 'days on market' PMs report, plus maintenance cost per door and the share of work orders closed on the first visit. Output is a one-page monthly report and a ready-to-send dispute email. An optional human bookkeeper review is the upsell.
why_now: Sept 2026 BiggerPockets threads show owners asking these exact questions with no tool that answers them. Landlord banking tools (Baselane, RentRedi) still 'aren't really bookkeeping', as one thread puts it. Extracting structured data from messy PM statement PDFs became cheap and reliable with current document-AI models. That turns a manual forensic accounting service into a $9-per-door product.
revenue_model: $9 per door per month, or $99 per property per year. A one-time $199 backfill audit of the trailing 12 months acts as the lead magnet and first revenue. A bookkeeper and CPA white-label plan at about $49 per client per month. The audit could later be paired with recovery: for any overcharge that gets refunded, take 15%.
non_obvious_insight: Owners are not asking for another PM platform. They want a neutral second set of eyes, and PMs will never build one because they are the party being checked. Evidence: 'How do you verify your PM net deposit matches the statement each month?' (19 replies) lists wrong-property charges, repairs with no invoice, and reserve adjustments that absorb shortfalls, at 5-10 minutes per property (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/899/topics/1293899-how-do-you-verify-your-pm-net-deposit-matches-the-statement-each-month). 'Every PM seems to send a different statement format, a different definition of net to owner' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1292833-owners-with-multiple-pms-how-do-you-keep-one-clean-view-across-statements). Owners can't verify whether a $400 repair needed $900, and 'days on market is not days vacant' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1301673-what-actually-keeps-out-of-state-landlords-up-at-night). A repair-transparency survey quote reads: 'I couldn't tell which line items were fair and which were padded' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1302340-small-landlords-with-a-pm-2-minute-survey-on-fees-and-repair-estimates).
first_30_days: Week 1: reply in the threads above and offer a free 12-month statement audit to 10 owners in exchange for anonymized statements. Build the audit by hand with a spreadsheet, an extraction prompt and a rules checklist. Weeks 2 to 3: deliver the audits, and use the discrepancies found as case studies. Week 4: convert to the $199 backfill and $9-per-door subscription, and pitch three real-estate bookkeepers on the white-label plan. Target: 10 paying owners and 2 bookkeeper partners.

title: Passive Elder Wellness Checks From Water Flow
one_liner: A daily 'your parent used water normally' text built from a clip-on flow sensor or a utility's smart-meter feed, sold to adult children as flood protection first and wellness second.
customer: Adult-child caregivers of solo-living 75+ parents and early-dementia patients (about $14/month), resold through home-care agencies and Area Agencies on Aging. Secondary buyers are water utilities with interval (AMI) meters that want a customer-care program.
problem: Wearables get abandoned, cameras get refused, and 69% of adults 50+ are uncomfortable sharing health data with AI tools. Yet 27% of Americans 65+ live alone, 59M family caregivers work unpaid, and agencies lose 77-80% of caregivers a year. China's 'Are You Dead?' check-in app topping paid charts in Jan 2026 shows families will pay for the thinnest possible 'are they OK' signal.
solution: A clip-on flow sensor on the main line, or opt-in utility interval data, plus fixture-signature disaggregation, learns each home's routine (first morning tap, flushes, showers, kitchen). It alerts on no morning use by a set hour, repeated 3 a.m. flushes (wandering), a tap left running, a sudden drop in showers (an early hygiene and dementia marker) and scald-level hot water. An optional auto-shutoff valve stops floods. The family gets a daily 'all normal' text, with an escalation tree to family, then the agency, then a welfare check.
why_now: Drought pressure has pushed utilities to roll out interval meters and customer portals for leak detection, so the data already exists. Medicaid cuts (about $911B) and shrinking Medicare Advantage benefits push more seniors onto unpaid family care. Older-adult tech acceptance is rising (23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, up from 10%). The 2026 China check-in app proved mass demand for minimalist check-ins.
revenue_model: $14/month per home plus a $79 kit. Agencies pay $6 per client per month for white-label. Utilities pay a license or revenue share of roughly $0.25-0.50 per enrolled account per month once AMI opt-in works.
non_obvious_insight: Water is the one utility no person can skip, fake or forget to charge, and no eldercare company sells it. It sidesteps the privacy and compliance objections that kill cameras and wearables. The 'leak and flood protection' pitch lets a proud parent accept something they would refuse as 'monitoring'. Japan's kettle-based 'mimamori' watch-over services showed appliance-use check-ins work, and water is the version that scales on utility infrastructure.
first_30_days: Buy 100 off-the-shelf clip-on flow monitors. Pitch three local home-care agencies and two caregiver Facebook groups a '$99 parent flood-and-check-in kit', and ship 50. Build the routine-anomaly model on consented data over 60-90 days. Then offer one small AMI-equipped utility an opt-in pilot using interval data.
